prompt: What kind of document is the PMBOK Guide?

choices.why: It is a book.
It is a professional body's guide, not a law.

choices.text: A guide to good practice, adapted by each organisation
choices.why: Right. It describes practice in a shared vocabulary; it is not a method adopted whole.

choices.text: A method adopted whole, with every process applied as written, like Scrum
choices.why: Organisations decide which parts they need.

prompt: Match each edition to how it is built.

pairs.right: Five process groups, ten knowledge areas, 49 processes
Twelve principles and eight performance domains

prompt: Put the four process groups that form the row in the figure in order.
trap: Planning comes before executing, and is revisited when execution teaches something.

prompt: A project has three phases. How many times does it go through the initiating process group?

choices.text: Never; initiating is only for programmes
choices.why: Projects and phases are initiated.

choices.text: Five times, once for each process group in the sixth edition
choices.why: The count of groups is unrelated to the number of phases.

choices.text: Once, at the start of the project
choices.why: That is the misreading of groups as phases.
Right. Each phase is initiated, planned, executed, controlled and closed.

prompt: Why does the figure draw monitoring and controlling as a band under the other groups?

choices.why: Right. It tracks progress from the first day to the last.
Monitoring after closing would be too late to act.

choices.text: It is optional in small projects
choices.why: The figure shows its timing, not whether it is optional.

choices.text: It belongs to the sponsor, not the project manager
choices.why: Ownership is not what the band shows.

prompt: Halfway through, a developer finds a requirement nobody understood. How does a PMBOK-style project change its plan, compared with Scrum?

choices.why: It can, through change control.
Right. Integrated change control: a request against the baseline, approved by somebody with authority; Scrum would replan at the next Sprint Planning.
A deviation is handled by changing the plan, not by restarting.

choices.text: The developer updates the plan directly
choices.why: Changes to a baseline go through change control.

prompt: Match each knowledge area to an example of its work.
How many knowledge areas does the sixth edition name?
hint: The table has one row each.

prompt: The schedule assumes a supplier delivers in March; the contract says June. Each document is correct on its own. Which knowledge area exists for this?

choices.text: Procurement, because a supplier is involved
choices.why: Procurement owns the contract, not its consistency with the schedule.
Each document is correct alone; the problem is the combination.
Telling people helps; holding the plan together is integration.
Right. It keeps scope, schedule, cost and contracts consistent with each other.

prompt: In PMBOK's vocabulary, where do an architect's non-functional requirements belong?
hint: How good it has to be.

choices.why: Documenting them is not what they are about.
They fit under quality.

choices.text: Integration, because they cross the whole system
choices.why: Crossing the system does not make them integration work.
Right. They are quality requirements, checked like any other.

prompt: Who issues the project charter?

choices.text: The development team, after estimating the work
choices.why: The team is not who authorises the project.
The charter gives the project manager authority; it comes from above.
Right. It authorises the project and gives the project manager authority.
PMI publishes the guide; it does not authorise projects.

prompt: What does the 100% rule of a work breakdown structure say?
hint: Each level against the one above.

choices.text: The budget must be fully allocated in week one
choices.why: Nothing about budget timing.

choices.text: All the team works 100% on one project
choices.why: It is about the tree, not about people.

choices.text: Every work package must be 100% done before the next starts
choices.why: That would be a sequencing rule; the 100% rule is about scope.

choices.text: Each level holds all the work of the level above, and nothing more
choices.why: Right. So the tree is exactly the project's scope.

prompt: Which of these is a well-formed branch of a WBS, by the lesson?

choices.why: Right. A thing that will exist.
A verb; activities come later.

choices.text: Testing everything thoroughly at the end
choices.why: An activity, and a late one.

choices.text: Meetings with the sponsor every Monday
choices.why: An activity, not a deliverable.

prompt: What does the lesson say is the real difference between a WBS and a product backlog?

choices.text: Only a WBS has a sponsor
choices.why: Who funds the work is a separate question.

choices.text: When the lower levels are filled in
choices.why: Right. A WBS is broken down during planning; a backlog just in time.
It can contain any deliverable.

choices.text: A backlog has no hierarchy at all, only a flat list of stories
choices.why: Epics, features and stories are levels.

prompt: How many days does the Agenda team's six-activity project take?
hint: The end of the forward pass.

prompt: How many days of slack does activity B, the slots API, have?
The team can save one day on either B or D. Which saves a day of the project?
hint: Which one is on the critical path?

choices.why: Every critical activity matters.

choices.text: Either; a day is a day
choices.why: Only days on the critical path move the end.
Right. D is critical; B already has a day of slack.
B has slack, so finishing it earlier moves nothing.

prompt: The six activities add up to 19 days of work, and the project takes 14. Why?

choices.text: Activity B is dropped from the plan
choices.why: B is done, in parallel with C and D.
The durations are as given; the overlap explains it.

choices.text: Some of the work runs in parallel
choices.why: Right. The longest path, not the total effort, sets the date.
All figures are working days already.

prompt: With EV of R$ 100,000 and AC of R$ 125,000, what is the cost performance index? Give two decimal places.
With a budget at completion of R$ 200,000 and a CPI of 0.80, what is the estimate at completion, in reais?
A project's SPI is 0.83 and its CPI is 0.80. What do they say?

choices.why: That would need indices above 1.

choices.text: Behind schedule but within budget, since spending is lower
choices.why: CPI below 1 means over budget.
Both are below 1. Close is not on plan; 0.80 is a 25% overspend per unit of work.
Right. Both indices are below 1, and they are read separately.

prompt: A team reports every work package as 90% done for weeks. What happens to its earned value, by the lesson?

choices.text: It becomes exact, since 90% is precise
choices.why: Precision in the number is not honesty in the measure.
The trouble is a flattering EV, not a specific CPI.

choices.text: Nothing; percent complete is what EV is built from
choices.why: EV built on 90% claims flatters the project.

choices.text: It looks nearly on plan while nothing finishes
choices.why: Right. That is why EV is counted by finished packages, 0% or 100%.

prompt: What idea ties the seventh edition together, according to the lesson?

choices.why: The seventh edition removed them.
Right. The approach is adapted to the project; the grid was never a checklist.
A scheduling technique, not the edition's theme.
Still a technique, not the organising idea.

prompt: Which of these are performance domains of the seventh edition? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: Yes.
A knowledge area of the sixth edition.
Yes.
Yes.
A process group of the sixth edition.

prompt: A job advert asks for 'experience following PMBOK'. What does the lesson advise you to find out?

choices.text: Whether they use the 49 processes in order
choices.why: The processes were never a sequence.

choices.text: Which edition, and so which way of working, they mean
choices.why: Right. Processes and baselines, or principles over an agile team.

choices.text: Nothing; PMBOK means the same everywhere
choices.why: The editions differ enough to describe different work.

choices.text: Whether the company is a PMI member
choices.why: Membership says little about how projects are run.

prompt: The activities with zero slack form the ___ path.
In week 6 a sponsor sees CPI 0.80 and an EAC of R$ 250,000 against a budget of R$ 200,000. Which response does earned value make possible that a final report would not?

choices.text: Acting while there is still time
choices.why: Right. Cutting scope, adding money or stopping are all still possible, because the forecast arrives while decisions can change the outcome.

choices.text: Raising the CPI by redefining the budget
choices.why: Changing the baseline hides the gap; it does not close it.
The numbers say the plan is not being met.

choices.text: Measuring whether the product is worth building
choices.why: Earned value does not measure that.
